title: Building a Text-to-Sign Language for Pakistani Urdu

body:
Many deaf Pakistanis rely on Pakistani Sign Language (PSL) to communicate. Unfortunately, there was no easy way to convert Urdu text into PSL images for this community. Existing research focuses on recognizing sign gestures and turning them into text or speech. Our project set out to reverse that process: given an Urdu letter, produce the corresponding hand-sign image in PSL. We call this “text to sign” generation, a sign language AI problem with real impact on accessibility. Under the guidance of Mr. Mian Saeed Akbar, our team (Wasif Ullah (Me), Muhammad Mubashir, Abdur Rahman) tackled this gap using modern deep learning.

The Data Challenge Hands with Messy Backgrounds

Figure: Typical hand-sign (the Ain ع). Early datasets had varied poses and busy backgrounds, which confused the model.

At first, we grabbed whatever PSL images we could find online (for example, the common “Ain ع” gesture above). But these initial datasets were low-res and inconsistent. Background clutter and uneven lighting made the model’s outputs blurry and noisy. In fact, when we first trained a GAN on this raw data, the generated signs looked smudged and unreliable. This failure taught us a lesson: to generate clear PSL visuals, we needed high-quality, clean training images.

So we built our own dataset. We captured over 200 high-resolution photos for each Urdu letter, with consistent lighting and framing. All pictures were manually labeled with the correct letter. Then we used Python and OpenCV/Pillow to preprocess: remove distracting backgrounds and make them clean. This dramatically boosted contrast between the hand and background (see the example image below), so the neural network could focus on hand shape instead of noise.

link of dataset: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/wasifullahcs/dataset-pakistani-sign-language

Figure: Clean PSL hand image helps the AI learn the hand shape clearly.

The cGAN Solution Conditional Image Generation

Next we designed a Conditional GAN (cGAN) to learn the mapping from Urdu letters to PSL images. In our implementation we used Python with TensorFlow/Keras and GPU acceleration. The generator network takes random noise plus an embedding of the Urdu character and produces a 128×128 hand-sign image. The discriminator network takes an image and its label and learns to classify real vs fake images. During training they compete: the generator tries to fool the discriminator by creating realistic signs, while the discriminator tries to catch fakes.

Figure: Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture. A generator network creates images, and a discriminator network judges real vs fake. In a conditional GAN, both networks are fed the target class (Urdu letter).

We trained this network on our cleaned PSL dataset for thousands of epochs. In practice the generator learned to conditionally produce the correct sign for each letter.

We also compared this to using a text-to-image diffusion model (Stable Diffusion). In our experiments, the cGAN outperformed diffusion. The diffusion model lacked precise label conditioning, so its sign images were often wrong or fuzzy. As one evaluation put it, “Stable Diffusion produced lower quality and less label-specific images compared to cGAN”. In short, cGAN gave us the control we needed to reliably generate each specific sign.

Tools and Tech Stack

Our entire pipeline was built with open-source tools. We coded the models in Python using TensorFlow/Keras. Image processing (cropping, resizing, background removal) was done with OpenCV and Pillow. For real-time deployment, we built a simple web interface using Streamlit (and Flask on the backend) so anyone can type Urdu letters and immediately see the generated PSL image. All these are common libraries in machine learning, showing how accessible such a system can be.

Results Clearer Signs, Better Scores

The effort paid off. Our final model produces sharper, more accurate hand-sign images for each Urdu letter. Empirically, the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) a standard metric where lower is better dropped dramatically after data cleaning. With the original online dataset the FID was around 190. After building our custom dataset it fell to ~130. With full preprocessing and more training it finally reached ~93. In other words, the generated images became far closer to real PSL images.

Figure: (Conceptual) Performance improvement chart. As training progressed, image quality (measured by FID score) improved steadily with our refined data and cGAN model.

Visually, the difference is clear. Below is a side-by-side comparison from our system:

  • Before cleaning: The GAN output had blurred outlines and messy backgrounds.
  • After our new data/preprocessing: The generated hand shapes are crisp and on a solid background, matching the intended sign.

Finally, we integrated everything into a Streamlit app. The end user just types an Urdu letter, and the corresponding PSL image appears instantly on screen. This real-time demo shows the system works end-to-end for any letter. We can even export the images as PNGs for use in teaching or communication tools.

Impact and Outlook

Our sign-generation system fills a critical technology gap in Pakistan’s accessibility landscape. It provides the first automated way to produce Pakistani Sign Language visuals from Urdu text. This can help educators create learning materials, or empower apps for the deaf. All of this was done with a lean setup and freely available tools (Python, TensorFlow, OpenCV, Streamlit).

Importantly, the success of our cGAN over diffusion highlights how the right model choice matters. By focusing on a conditional GAN, we maintained control over each output sign, producing consistent, label-specific images. This work shows that even with limited data (hundreds of images per sign), a carefully built cGAN can achieve strong performance in sign generation.

Looking forward, our prototype can be extended to full words or phrases, or combined with ASL/PSL video generators. But even now, we have a working proof-of-concept system. As a team (Wasif Ullah, Muhammad Mubashir, Abdur Rahman under supervisor Mian Saeed Akbar), we’re proud to offer this tool to developers and accessibility advocates in Pakistan. By opening up “text to sign” translation for Urdu, we hope to make technology more inclusive for our hearing-impaired community.

All source code and images were developed using Python (TensorFlow/Keras, OpenCV) and deployed via a Streamlit web interface. This project was a collaboration of Wasif Ullah, Muhammad Mubashir, and Abdur Rahman, supervised by Mr. Mian Saeed Akbar at UET Mardan.
